title: A vortex street is read as a sign pattern: thin attached layers, then alternating eddies at a fixed spacing
summary: The vorticity map of flow past a cylinder shows two thin layers of opposite sign on the body and a row of alternating eddies downstream. Reading it means checking the colour scale, the sign of each layer, the eddy spacing and the time at which the map was taken.

media.alt: Vorticity map of flow past a circular cylinder at Re = 100, t = 80, axes x over D (0 to 16) and y over D (0 to 10), red-blue colour bar from minus 20 to 20. The cylinder near x = 3.2, y = 5 has a strong red layer on its lower left and a blue layer on top. Downstream, pale alternating vortices appear: blue near x = 6.8, red near x = 9.8, blue near x = 13. The rest of the domain is neutral grey.

read_the_figure.question: Has the wake developed the alternating vortex street expected at this Reynolds number, and where are the eddies and their spacing?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y: position in units of the cylinder diameter D, with the flow from left to right. Colour: vorticity (red positive, counter-clockwise; blue negative, clockwise), on a symmetric scale from about minus 20 to plus 20, labelled in 1/s.
look_at: Locate the cylinder (a circle near x = 3.2, y = 5). The strongest colours are on its surface: the thin layers where the flow is brought to rest.
Check the sign pattern: the layer on top is blue and the layer below is red. Fluid above the body speeds up with height, which gives negative vorticity; below, the opposite.
Follow the wake: pale alternating eddies, blue, red, blue, at x of about 6.8, 9.8 and 13. Same-sign eddies are about 6 diameters apart; successive opposite-sign ones about 3.

The eddies are pale because the colour scale is set by the thin layers on the body, which carry much larger vorticity. Weak colours do not mean weak eddies; they mean a scale dominated by the wall layer.
Look at the lateral position: the eddies sit slightly above and below the centreline in a staggered pattern, which is the street.
Read the title time (t = 80) and relate it to the force history: shedding is fully developed after about t = 40.
read_the_figure.proves: A staggered row of opposite-sign eddies with regular spacing, behind a body with signed shear layers of the expected orientation, shows that the unsteady wake has formed. The picture alone does not give the frequency or the forces; those come from the time series.
if_wrong: A symmetric, steady pair of attached eddies at a late time: shedding has not started; the run is too short or the flow is below the critical Reynolds number.
An asymmetric pattern that does not repeat: numerical noise or a restrictive domain.
Eddies that vanish a few diameters downstream: excessive numerical diffusion or a coarse outflow region.
Colour limits chosen so that the wake looks empty: rescale to a lower maximum to see the street.
must_check: The colour scale is symmetric and its limits are stated; the eddies are clipped or pale if the scale is dominated by the wall layer.
Axes are in units of D and the aspect ratio is equal, so circles look like circles.
The time of the snapshot relative to the onset of shedding.
The domain height and distance to the outflow, so confinement is known (here the domain is about 10 diameters tall).
Resolution: at least a few cells across the wall layer.
as_drawn: Colour bar about minus 20 to plus 20; wall-layer colours near the limits, wake eddies about 3 to 5 in magnitude.
Blue eddies near x of 6.8 and 12.9, red eddy near 9.8: same-sign spacing about 6.1 D, alternating spacing about 3 D.
Domain about 16 D long and 10 D tall; cylinder centre near x = 3.2 D, y = 5 D.
Animation poster (t = 2.64): two thin symmetric layers (blue above, red below) wrapped around the cylinder and a short pale attached region behind it; colour limits about plus or minus 25.

terms.meaning: Two staggered rows of opposite-sign vortices shed alternately from the two sides of a bluff body.
A thin layer where velocity changes rapidly across the flow. It contains strong vorticity of one sign and rolls up into vortices.
For flow left to right, positive vorticity is counter-clockwise. Fluid above a wall layer that speeds up with height has negative vorticity.
The integral of vorticity over an area: the total strength of a vortex.
The streamwise distance between successive same-sign vortices.
The speed at which the street moves downstream: wavelength times shedding frequency.
Starting the flow suddenly from rest, which first creates symmetric attached layers and only later the street.
When values beyond the colour limits all get the same colour, which hides their differences.

remember: Thin wall layers have much larger vorticity than the wake eddies; a map scaled to them shows the wake pale.
Opposite-sign vortices alternate: spacing between opposite signs is half the same-sign wavelength.
U_c = lambda f = St (lambda / D) U in units of the free-stream speed.
The wall layer thickness scales like D over the square root of Re.
Shedding starts after an instability phase; early frames are symmetric.
A snapshot has no frequency; combine it with a time series.

understand.title: A still and a movie of the same case
understand.text: The still at t = 80 shows the developed street; the movie starts at t = 0 with the symmetric attached layers of the impulsive start and, in its later frames, runs through the growth of the asymmetry to the street. The two together show the sequence that the force history records as a lift curve that is flat and then grows. Read the movie against the force figure: the instability sets in around t = 30 to 40.

understand.title: Why the colour scale matters here
understand.text: The wall layers carry order 20 vorticity and the eddies order 3 to 5. A map scaled to the maximum will always show a pale wake, and a map scaled to the wake would saturate at the wall. Neither is wrong, but the choice should be visible; a second panel at a lower limit, or a symmetric log scale, would show both.

understand.title: What the street spacing tells you
understand.text: The wavelength and the shedding frequency together give the speed at which the eddies travel. A convection speed close to but below the free-stream speed is the usual outcome. A very different value would indicate that the frequency and the picture do not belong to the same flow, for example because of a different blockage.

steps.title: Why the signs are what they are
steps.tex: \omega=\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y},\qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial y}>0\text{ above the wall layer}\;\Rightarrow\;\omega<0
steps.note: With flow left to right, the speed rises from zero at the body to the free-stream value above it, so the vertical shear is positive and the vorticity negative (blue). Below the body the shear is reversed (red). The street is made of the two layers detaching alternately.

steps.title: Alternating spacing is half the wavelength
steps.note: Staggered rows: every second eddy has the same sign. In the figure the red eddy lies about half-way between the two blue ones.

steps.title: Convection speed of the street
steps.note: Using the Strouhal number printed on the force-history figure for the same case. A value a little below one is expected, since eddies are carried by the wake flow, which is slower than the free stream. The reading error in the spacing is a few tenths of a diameter, so only the first digit is meaningful.

steps.title: Thickness of the wall layer
steps.note: Order-of-magnitude boundary-layer scaling. At the finer resolution of the project's grid study there are only about three cells across the layer, which is why the layer is a few pixels wide in the map and why force results depend on resolution.

steps.title: Circulation of an eddy
steps.note: Colour is vorticity density; the strength of an eddy is the integral over its area. A pale but wide eddy can carry as much circulation as a small intense one.

steps.title: Saturating a colour scale
steps.note: All values beyond the limits receive the end colour. Choose the limit from the quantity of interest and state it; an animation must keep it fixed (the poster has limits near 25, the still near 20).

worked.title: Eddy convection speed from the map and the force history
worked.problem: Same-sign eddies are 6.1 diameters apart in the map. The force history of the same case gives a Strouhal number of 0.1495. What speed do the eddies travel at, relative to the free stream?

solution.text: Frequency from the Strouhal number, in units of U over D.

worked.answer: About 0.91 times the free-stream speed, plausible for a street (less than the free stream); the third digit is not meaningful given the reading error of the spacing.

analyze.q: The street eddies are pale in the map. What two plotting changes would make them clearer, and what would each cost?
analyze.hint: A lower symmetric limit saturates the wall layer; a symmetric log scale compresses amplitudes.

analyze.q: Suppose the map at t = 80 showed an exactly symmetric attached pair behind the cylinder. List three reasons, and say which check on the force history would identify each.
analyze.hint: Run too short, below critical Re, numerical damping of the instability.

analyze.q: Compare the poster frame of the movie (t = 2.64) with the still: what physical process links them, and what determines the time it takes?
analyze.hint: Growth rate of the wake instability.

evaluate.q: Does the still image alone show that the solver is accurate at this Reynolds number? What else do you need?
evaluate.hint: Frequency, forces and reference values at the same blockage.

evaluate.q: The movie shows a fixed colour scale. Why is this essential for comparing early and late frames?
evaluate.hint: Per-frame autoscaling hides growth and decay.

create: Draw a two-panel version of the still: the same data with the full scale on the left and a scale of about one fifth on the right, with the cylinder outlined, so that wall layer and street can both be read.
Design a one-line annotation for the animation that prints the time, the lift coefficient and a marker for the onset of shedding.

checks.q: Why is the layer on top of the cylinder blue?
checks.hint: Sign of the vertical shear above the body.
checks.answer: Above the body the speed rises with height, so the shear du/dy is positive and the vorticity, minus du/dy plus dv/dx, is negative, which the diverging map draws in blue.

checks.q: Same-sign eddies are 5.5 diameters apart and the Strouhal number is 0.16. What is the convection speed in units of the free stream?
The wake eddies look pale but the force history shows large lift oscillations. Is that a contradiction?
checks.answer: Not necessarily. The colour scale is set by the thin wall layers, so the eddies look pale while they still carry circulation over a large area. The lift depends on the flow around the body, not on how bright the wake looks.

checks.q: A reader says the eddy spacing proves the Strouhal number is right. Respond.
checks.hint: Spacing and frequency are linked by the convection speed.
checks.answer: Spacing alone does not fix the frequency; it also depends on the convection speed. They agree if the speed is plausible, which is a consistency check, not a proof. The Strouhal number must be measured from the force or velocity time series.

checks.q: How would you quantify the street wavelength objectively instead of by eye?
checks.hint: A spatial correlation or spectrum along the wake axis.
checks.answer: Sample the vorticity or the transverse velocity along a line parallel to the wake axis, compute its autocorrelation or Fourier spectrum, and take the first non-zero peak of the autocorrelation or the dominant wavenumber as the wavelength, with a spread over several snapshots.
